title: Kyrie Irving Says The WNBA Needs More Black Head Coaches
htmlContent:
Kyrie Irving has long been one of the NBA's most vocal WNBA supporters. In a recent interview, the Dallas Mavericks star was asked whether he would like to see Black women get more chances to lead WNBA teams. His answer was direct.

"Yeah, I think there's definitely a big desire for more Black female head coaches to be involved in the W," Irving told LandonBuford.com. "You're just seeing the league grow tremendously, and I think a lot of the social issues that are talked about are very relevant, and they need to be talked about. So I'm grateful you asked that question."

He also praised the players for standing together.

"I think the W in general just does a great job of staying connected, staying united, doing things for each other and advocating for the things that they want," he said. "So I'm really proud of our women, really proud of my sisters over there. But we definitely do need to see a lot more Black head coaches over there."

Kobe's Love for the W

Irving was also asked whether he and the late Kobe Bryant, his close friend and mentor, ever discussed the topic.

"No, we never got a chance to talk about those specifics," Irving said. "But definitely, echoing your statement, Kobe was in love with the W and wanted to see it grow and expand."

Irving framed the issue around fairness and qualifications.

"There are a lot of racial components that could muddy the water a little bit, but we're just talking about the greatness and what people are qualified to do and what their résumé says they're qualified to do," he said. "If you're qualified for the job, you should get it. So as long as that's an equal opportunity, then we're all good."

A League Without a Black Woman on the Sideline

Irving's comments come at a notable moment for the WNBA. The Seattle Storm declined to renew Noelle Quinn's contract after the 2025 season, and the 2026 season tipped off without a single Black woman serving as a head coach. It was only the third time that has happened, after 2006 and 2020.

Black women make up a large majority of WNBA players, yet the only Black head coaches in 2026 were two men: Tyler Marsh of the Chicago Sky and Sydney Johnson of the Washington Mystics.

Paige Bueckers Adds Her Voice

Irving is not alone. After the Dallas Wings beat the Chicago Sky 96-91 in July, Wings starPaige Bueckers was asked by LandonBuford.com about the lack of Black women head coaches in the league.

"The WNBA was built on a lot of Black women," Bueckers said. "It's definitely right for them to get the same equal opportunity as everybody else."

She called for "equal opportunity and no discrimination based on what you look like, who you like, and anything of that nature."

Bueckers, who is white, explained why the issue is personal to her.

"I grew up with a lot of prominent Black women in my life that were very important to me in how I was raised and how I grew up, being my stepmom, my AAU coach," she said. "So I understand how amazing they are and how they should get the same equal opportunity as a white woman, as a white man to be an important piece of this league."

Noelle Quinn on the Weight of Representation

During the 2025 season, Quinn was the only Black woman leading a WNBA team, and she spoke openly about what that meant.

"It's important. It does get heavy sometimes, and I don't talk about it often in front of you all," she said. "But it's truly an honor, and I'm grateful. Still, to be one of only 13 [head coaches], it carries weight."

Quinn stressed how much she relied on the people around her.

"To have Pooh, who is down the street in Portland, obviously my staff, my circle, my family, and my team, it is important," she said. "I have to lean on the people who really know me and pour into me, and that support is reciprocated and much appreciated."

Pooh Jeter and the Power of Community

The Pooh she mentioned is former Portland Trail Blazers assistant coach Pooh Jeter, who attended a Storm game that season to show his support. He told LandonBuford.com that the visit was personal.

"Noelle and I have known each other since we were young," Jeter said. "But what people might not know is that Ebony Hoffman, who's on the staff, is actually my cousin."

Jeter also pointed to Quinn's ties to the Black Coaches Association.

"You never really know what's going on in people's lives, but we always try to find ways to bring joy to one another," he said.

Where the Conversation Goes From Here

Quinn has since coached in the Unrivaled league, but the WNBA still has no Black women at the helm. With Irving and Bueckers pushing the issue into the spotlight, the pressure on front offices is growing. As Irving put it, if you are qualified for the job, you should get a fair shot.
excerpt: Kyrie Irving, Paige Bueckers, Noelle Quinn, and Pooh Jeter have all spoken out about the lack of Black women head coaches in the WNBA, as the 2026 season tipped off without a single Black woman on the sideline for only the third time in league history.
